`_DOC_EXTENSIONS_SET` / `_DOC_EXTENSIONS` are computed here but never used anywhere in this module ( `_file_category()` defaults to "doc" without consulting `_DOC_EXTENSIONS`). Consider removing the unused import and set to avoid dead code / potential lint failures, or update `_file_category()` to explicitly use `_DOC_EXTENSIONS` if that’s the intent.
```suggestion
    PAPER_EXTENSIONS as _PAPER_EXTENSIONS_SET,
    IMAGE_EXTENSIONS as _IMAGE_EXTENSIONS_SET,
)
# Strip dots for suffix-based matching in _file_category
_CODE_EXTENSIONS = {ext.lstrip(".") for ext in _CODE_EXTENSIONS_SET}

The `_safe_rel()` docstring/comment says the fallback path will "log the unknown type", but the implementation never logs anything. Either add a log statement when `candidate` isn’t in `_ALLOWED_RELATION_TYPES`, or remove the logging claim to keep the code/documentation consistent.
```suggestion
        # Fallback: return the sanitized value if it is still a valid relationship type
```

`module_defn` node IDs are generated from `(stem, mod_name)` only. For nested modules (or multiple modules with the same name in one file), this can collide and merge distinct modules into a single node. Consider including the parent/container id in the module id (e.g., derive `mod_nid` from `parent_nid`/`module_nid`), so module identities remain unique within a file.
```suggestion
                mod_nid = _make_id(parent_nid, mod_name)
```

Type nodes (`union_type_defn` / `record_type_defn` / `type_abbrev_defn`) use `_make_id(stem, name)` even when extracted inside a module. This can collapse same-named types declared in different modules within the same file into one node. Consider namespacing the type id by the container (`parent_nid`/`module_nid`) similar to how functions are namespaced.
```suggestion
                type_nid = _make_id(module_nid, name) if module_nid else _make_id(stem, name)
```

F# support is added to the default dispatch map even when the optional `tree_sitter_fsharp` binding is not installed. In that case `extract_fsharp()` returns an `error`, but `extract()` currently drops that information, so users can end up with silently-missing nodes/edges for `.fs/.fsx` files. Consider either (1) gating `.fs/.fsx` dispatch on the dependency being available, or (2) collecting and printing/logging extractor errors once per run so the missing support is visible.
```suggestion
    }
    if importlib.util.find_spec("tree_sitter_fsharp") is not None:
        _DISPATCH[".fs"] = extract_fsharp
        _DISPATCH[".fsx"] = extract_fsharp
```

There are extensive per-language extractor tests (e.g., `tests/test_languages.py`) and fixtures for other languages, but this PR adds a new `extract_fsharp()` without adding any F# fixture/tests. Adding at least a small `.fs` fixture plus assertions for definitions + call edges would help prevent regressions in the custom two-pass walk logic.

`fsharp = ["tree-sitter-fsharp"]` adds an installable extra, but the PR description notes Python bindings for the grammar may not be published to PyPI. If that’s the case, `pip install .[fsharp]` will fail for users. Consider switching this extra to a VCS/URL dependency (or documenting build/install steps clearly) until a PyPI package is available.
```suggestion

Structural node IDs are likely to collide across files: file nodes use only `path.stem` and section nodes use only the heading title. This will merge unrelated files/sections that share names (e.g., multiple `README.md` or `Introduction` headings), and in prose mode it can also collide with semantic concept IDs (which are also snake_case), causing semantic nodes to be dropped during the merge-by-id step. Use a separate namespace for structural nodes (e.g., `file__<rel_path>` and `section__<rel_path>__<heading>`) or incorporate the relative path into the ID so every file/section is uniquely addressable while keeping semantic concept IDs clean.

`_make_id()` can return an empty string for headings comprised entirely of non-ASCII characters or punctuation (after the regex cleanup). That would create nodes with empty IDs and cause massive collisions. Consider adding a fallback (e.g., a short hash of the original text/parts) when the normalized result is empty.

The module-level docstring says this parser handles PDF and DOCX and parses headings/sections/paragraphs, but `_read_file()` currently returns an empty string for `.pdf`/`.docx` and the structural parser only extracts headings (no paragraphs). Either adjust the docstring to match the actual behavior or add real structural extraction support for those formats.
```suggestion
handles text-based non-code corpora that can be read directly here: markdown, plain
text, reStructuredText, and Jupyter notebooks. It deterministically parses document
structure such as headings/sections and builds a structural graph without any LLM calls.

PDF and DOCX files may be recognized by the broader prose pipeline, but this module
does not perform built-in structural text extraction for those formats in `_read_file()`.
```

YAML frontmatter stripping is too naive: `text.find('---', 3)` can match a thematic break (`---`) later in the body, truncating content incorrectly. It’s safer to only treat frontmatter as closed by a delimiter on its own line (e.g., search for `
---
` from the start) and strip exactly the first frontmatter block.
```suggestion
    # Strip only an initial YAML frontmatter block delimited by standalone lines.
    if text.startswith("---
"):
        end = text.find("
---
", 5)
        if end != -1:
            text = text[end + len("
---
"):]
    elif text.startswith("---
"):
        end = text.find("
---
", 4)
        if end != -1:
            text = text[end + len("
---
"):]
```

In `_read_ipynb()`, `cell['source']` can be either a list of strings or a single string depending on how the notebook was written. Using `"".join(...)` on a string will join characters and corrupt the content. Normalize `source` first (e.g., if it’s a list join it, if it’s a string use it as-is).

This new extraction path doesn’t appear to have any automated tests yet. Since the repo has a comprehensive `tests/` suite (including fixtures like `tests/fixtures/sample.md`), please add unit tests for `extract_prose()` covering at least: (1) markdown heading extraction + contains edges, (2) YAML frontmatter stripping behavior, and (3) ID uniqueness/collision behavior across multiple files.

The embedded `python -c` block is currently indented (e.g., it starts with `␠import sys`). When passed to `python -c`, leading indentation at top level triggers `IndentationError: unexpected indent`, so the hook will fail immediately. Remove the leading whitespace from the Python snippet (or switch to a heredoc / explicit dedent) so the first line starts at column 0.

The header comment now says the hook "auto-rebuilds the knowledge graph" with no qualifier, but the hook still calls `graphify.watch._rebuild_code`, which only rebuilds the *code* graph and does not set the `graphify-out/needs_update` flag for doc/paper/image changes. This is misleading for users who expect non-code edits to be reflected. Consider rewording to "code graph" (and/or invoking the same `_notify_only`/flag behavior when non-code files changed).
```suggestion
# Auto-rebuilds the code graph after each commit (no LLM needed).
# Installed by: graphify hook install
#
# Why no extension filter: _rebuild_code internally calls detect() which
# rescans the project from scratch using the authoritative CODE_EXTENSIONS
# set in graphify/detect.py. A hook-side filter would only gate WHETHER the
# code-graph rebuild fires, not WHAT gets rebuilt — and any hardcoded copy
# here drifts from the real allowlist (.tsx/.jsx/.lua/.ex/.jl/... were
# missed in the past). The rebuild is cheap (~2s, no LLM), so just always
# run it. Output is appended to graphify-out/.hook.log so silent failures
# stay visible.
```

There are tests for hook install/uninstall, but nothing asserts that the generated post-commit hook is syntactically valid (e.g., that the embedded `python -c` snippet isn't accidentally indented) or that logging is configured as expected. Adding a focused test that inspects the installed hook content for these invariants would prevent regressions like this indentation issue from shipping again.

Typo in the filename: this section says the install writes to `AGETNTS.md`, but the project convention/CLI uses `AGENTS.md`. As written, users may look for/edit the wrong file.
```suggestion
This writes a `## graphify` section to the local `AGENTS.md` that instructs Codex to check the graph before answering codebase questions and rebuild it after code changes. No manual `/graphify` needed in future sessions.
```

The benchmark CLI’s non-.json error message differs from the shared loader (_load_graph) (capitalization/wording). Consider reusing the same wording (or factoring a shared helper) so user-facing errors are consistent across `query`, `serve`, and `benchmark`.

The new `benchmark` CLI behavior rejects non-`.json` paths, but there’s no regression test covering this branch (current tests only cover the “outside graphify-out/” rejection). Adding a test for a non-`.json` argument (e.g., `graphify benchmark graphify-out/graph.txt`) would prevent this validation from being accidentally removed later.

The uninstall messaging is now misleading: when AGENTS.md is missing or the marker isn’t present, this function prints "nothing to do" but still performs platform-owned cleanup (e.g., removing the OpenCode plugin or Codex hook). Consider adjusting the message(s) to reflect that platform cleanup may still occur (or gate the message on platform), so `graphify opencode uninstall` doesn’t claim it did nothing while it actually removed plugin state.

_PLATFORM_CONFIG sets "skill_file": "skill.md" which is the Claude Code skill. It references `spawn_agent` and Claude-specific tooling that doesn't exist in Kiro. Should use a Kiro-specific skill file (like skill-kiro.md) that references use_subagent `/InvokeSubagents` — Kiro's actual parallel dispatch mechanism.
We should add tests for this integration like there are for other platforms.

The igraph normalization for **edge** betweenness is using the node-betweenness scaling factor `((n-1)(n-2))`, which does not match NetworkX’s `edge_betweenness_centrality(..., normalized=True)` normalization. This will violate the PR’s “drop-in replacement / same normalization” contract for edge betweenness. Adjust the scale factor to match NetworkX’s edge normalization so igraph and NX outputs are comparable.

This assumes `G.edges[nid, neighbor]` is a flat attribute dict; on `nx.MultiGraph`/`nx.MultiDiGraph` it’s a mapping of edge keys → dict, so `.get("relation")` will not work (and can throw). `_subgraph_to_text()` already contains a MultiGraph-safe pattern—use the same approach here to select an actual edge attribute dict before reading `relation`/`confidence`.

Similar to `get_neighbors`, `edata = G.edges[u, v]` will not be a single attribute dict on MultiGraphs. If MultiGraphs are supported elsewhere (and `_subgraph_to_text()` now handles them), this path rendering should also select a concrete edge attribute dict (e.g., first key’s attributes) before calling `.get(...)`.

Similar to `get_neighbors`, `edata = G.edges[u, v]` will not be a single attribute dict on MultiGraphs. If MultiGraphs are supported elsewhere (and `_subgraph_to_text()` now handles them), this path rendering should also select a concrete edge attribute dict (e.g., first key’s attributes) before calling `.get(...)`.

`_load_graph()` no longer uses `validate_graph_path()`, which weakens the “only load graphs from graphify-out/” guard described in the security model and reintroduces a broader local-file read surface if an untrusted caller can influence the server launch args. Consider using `validate_graph_path(graph_path)` (with the updated base auto-discovery in `security.py`) so behavior matches the intended threat model.

The regex char class appears to remove `]` but not `[` (because `[\]]` only matches `]`). If labels can contain `[` it may still produce filenames/wikilinks that Obsidian treats as markup and can break navigation. Update the regex to explicitly strip both `[` and `]` and keep it aligned with the actual `export.safe_name` implementation (since the docstring claims they mirror each other).

`sanitize_label()` no longer HTML-escapes (per `graphify/security.py`), so this mitigation description is now inaccurate. Update SECURITY.md to reflect the new contract (and ensure HTML-producing callers escape at the point of injection).

The PR title/description are narrowly framed around “use igraph C backend for betweenness centrality,” but this PR also includes a package rename/version bump, new modules (transcription, hooks, wiki), major detection/watch/serve/security changes, and large documentation additions. Consider splitting into separate PRs or updating the PR title/description to match the actual scope so reviewers can evaluate risk and intent accurately.

In the igraph edge betweenness path, the normalization scale is using the node-betweenness denominator ((n-1)*(n-2) with an extra /2 for undirected). NetworkX edge_betweenness_centrality uses a different normalization (based on n*(n-1), with a factor of 2 for undirected), so this will return values that don’t match the fallback NX code and can exceed 1 on small graphs. Adjust the scaling to match NetworkX’s edge betweenness normalization (or use igraph’s built-in normalization if available) so the helper is truly drop-in.

The normalization explanation here is internally inconsistent and appears incorrect for NetworkX: for undirected graphs, NetworkX’s normalized betweenness centrality applies a factor of 2/((n-1)(n-2)), not 1/((n-1)(n-2)). Please fix the comment (and double-check the scaling logic against NetworkX’s definition) to avoid future confusion.

The sampled NetworkX fallback path uses randomness but doesn’t pass a seed, so results can change between runs when igraph isn’t installed and the graph is > _SAMPLE_THRESHOLD. Consider passing a fixed seed (and doing the same in the edge-betweenness fallback) to keep outputs stable and avoid hard-to-debug diffs in generated reports.

This import was moved into the middle of the module. Keeping imports at the top-level import section improves readability and avoids subtle import-order/circular-import surprises. Consider moving this `from graphify.detect import ...` up with the other imports at the top of the file.

The `_src`/`_tgt` resolution + fallback-to-(u,v) pattern is now duplicated in multiple places (_cross_file_surprises, _cross_community_surprises, suggest_questions). Consider extracting a small helper to resolve safe endpoint ids from edge data to reduce repetition and keep the behavior consistent if it needs to change again.

New fast-centrality helpers introduce several behavior branches (igraph exact, NX exact, NX sampled). There are existing pytest tests for analyze.py, but nothing here asserts equivalence/normalization vs NetworkX (especially for edge betweenness) or verifies the threshold/seed behavior. Adding focused unit tests (with igraph-import mocked/unavailable and small synthetic graphs) would prevent regressions and validate the “drop-in replacement” claim.

Step 1 writes the interpreter path to `graphify-out/.graphify_python`, but Step 2 (and many later bash blocks) run `$(cat .graphify_python) ...`. As written, `cat .graphify_python` will fail and all subsequent commands will use the wrong interpreter. Make the path consistent by either writing `.graphify_python` in the project root, or updating every `$(cat .graphify_python)` reference to `$(cat graphify-out/.graphify_python)`.
```suggestion
**In every subsequent bash block, replace `python3` with `$(cat graphify-out/.graphify_python)` to use the correct interpreter.**

### Step 2 - Detect files

```bash
$(cat graphify-out/.graphify_python) -c "
```

Step 2 writes detect output to `.graphify_detect.json` in the project root, but Step 2.5 reads `graphify-out/.graphify_detect.json` for transcription. That mismatch will break video/audio transcription on Pi. Align the detect output location and all subsequent reads to a single path (preferably under `graphify-out/` like other artifacts).

This section still instructs semantic extraction via parallel subagents, but the Pi note says extraction is sequential (no multi-agent). That’s contradictory guidance for Pi and can cause the wrong workflow to be followed. Gate the subagent/parallel instructions to non-Pi platforms, or rewrite Part B here to describe only the sequential Pi flow.

`_pi_install()` calls `install(platform="pi")`, which prints the post-install hint "For a native /graphify alias inside a project, run: graphify pi install". When the user is already running `graphify pi install`, this becomes confusing/self-referential output. Consider refactoring `install()` to allow suppressing the Pi-specific hint when invoked from `_pi_install()`, or extract a lower-level "copy skill file" helper that `_pi_install()` can call without the interactive guidance prints.

`target = lsp_edge.get("target", "")` permits empty-string targets ("defines" edges) which then flow into graph edges. Graphify’s graph format expects edges to reference real node IDs; empty targets create dangling/invalid edges. For "defines", consider using the file node ID as target, or model it as a node attribute instead of an edge.

Because `extract_from_file()` bails out when `language not in self.PATTERNS`, any file extensions mapped to languages without patterns (e.g. typescript/go/rust in `detect_language`) are silently skipped. Consider either constraining `detect_language` to supported patterns or emitting a warning when a requested language has no patterns.

`if all_lsp_edges or not_started_servers:` references `not_started_servers`, which is not defined (the variable above is named `not_started`). This will raise NameError when no LSP edges were found. Use `not_started` (or similar) here, and add a unit test for the no-edges / some-servers-failed path.
```suggestion
        if all_lsp_edges or not_started:
```

No tests cover the new `lsp-import` command routing or the static enhancer’s graph mutation behavior (deduplication, placeholder nodes, metadata updates). The repo has extensive pytest coverage for other commands; adding at least a smoke test that runs the command against a small fixture graph would help prevent regressions.

The generic `direct_call` regex will also match function definition lines (e.g. `def foo(...` / `function foo(`), producing self-call edges (`foo` calls `foo`) at every definition site. Consider skipping call extraction on lines that matched a definition pattern, or tightening the call regex (e.g., negative lookbehind for `def\s` / `function\s`) to avoid polluting the call graph.

`current_function` is set when a definition line is seen but never cleared when leaving that function’s scope, so any subsequent top-level code (after the last function) will be attributed as calls from the last defined function. If you want reasonable caller attribution, consider tracking indentation (python) / `end` blocks (lua) to reset scope, or fall back to the file node when outside a function body.

In the python patterns, `method_def` uses the same regex as `function_def` (only 1 capture group), but the `method_def` branch unconditionally accesses `match.group(2)`, which will raise an IndexError on any python `def ...` line. Either remove `method_def` for python, or use a regex that captures the class/receiver context (or treat python methods the same as functions here).

`caller = current_function or f"{file_stem}_file"` will not match Graphify’s file node IDs (AST extraction uses `_make_id(str(path))`, not `<stem>_file`). This will produce edges whose `source` node doesn’t exist in `graph.json`, so they’ll be ignored by `build_from_json()` and/or create dangling endpoints in the JSON. Consider using the same ID normalization as `extract._make_id(str(file_path))` (or look up the file node ID from the existing graph by `source_file`).

For python `string_import` matches, `match.groups()` is always length 2 with one side being None (due to alternation). `callee = groups[1] if len(groups) > 1 else groups[0]` therefore often selects None (e.g., `from x import y`). Pick the first non-empty group instead so imports resolve consistently.
```suggestion
                            # require("module") / import ... from "module"
                            callee = next((group for group in groups if group), None)
```

`detect_language()` returns "typescript" for .ts/.tsx, but `PATTERNS` has no "typescript" entry, so TypeScript extraction will never run. Either map typescript to the javascript patterns or add a dedicated `PATTERNS["typescript"]` entry, and keep the CLI `--language` choices in sync.
```suggestion
            ".ts": "javascript",
            ".tsx": "javascript",
```

`target_exists = any(...)` scans all nodes for every edge, making `add_edges()` O(E·N). With the node/edge counts shown in the PR description this can become a noticeable bottleneck. Build a `set` of existing node IDs once (and update it when adding placeholder nodes) to make the check O(1).

The help text says `lsp-import` "enhance graph with LSP references", but the command currently delegates to `lsp_enhance_static` (regex-based static analysis). Please align the CLI description/options with the actual implementation (or route to `lsp_enhance` when available and fall back to static), otherwise users will install LSP servers expecting them to be used.
```suggestion
        print("  lsp-import [path]       enhance graph with static source references (regex-based analysis)")
        print("    --graph <path>          path to graph.json (default graphify-out/graph.json)")
        print("    --language <lang>       specific language(s) to process (default: auto-detect)")
        print("    --dry-run               extract data without modifying graph")
        print("    --list-languages        show supported languages for static analysis")
```

# Bug: Step 0 vocab tokens silently dropped by Step 1's length filter

**Step 0 extracts tokens with a minimum length of 3:**

```
if 3 <= len(t) <= 30:
    vocab.add(t)
```
**But the inline traversal in Step 1 filters with:**
```
terms = [t.lower() for t in question.split() if len(t) > 3]
```

> len(t) > 3 means minimum 4 characters. So any 3-char token that Step 0 deliberately selected from the graph vocab **_(api, tok, auth, use, get)_** gets silently dropped here before the BFS/DFS even starts.

## **Suggested fix**:
Since the QUESTION passed into Step 1 is already the space-joined output of Step 0 (vocab-constrained, quality-filtered), the length check is redundant and harmful here:

```
terms = [t.lower() for t in question.split()]
```
If you want to keep some noise filtering, at minimum align with Step 0's threshold:
```
terms = [t.lower() for t in question.split() if len(t) >= 3]
```
Fixed in 5643c7f — changed `len(t) > 3` to `len(t) >= 3` on line 49 to align Step 1 with Step 0's threshold. Thanks for catching this!

The PR title implies "security fixes & updates", but this document is an audit report (findings + suggested remediations). Adding an explicit note that no remediations are included in this PR will reduce reviewer confusion.

Finding 1 currently asserts that a payload like `A} DETACH DELETE n //` could survive sanitization and produce a destructive Cypher query. In the current implementation, `_safe_label` strips non `[A-Za-z0-9_]` characters and `_safe_rel` replaces non `[A-Z0-9_]` with `_`, so the example payload would be reduced to a safe identifier (though silently coerced). Consider rephrasing this as "silent coercion / potential syntax error" risk rather than a destructive injection example.

Finding 2 says the CLI prefers env-var auth but doesn't mention that `push_password` is already sourced from `NEO4J_PASSWORD`/`FALKORDB_PASSWORD` by default and only overridden when `--password` is supplied. Clarifying this in the text would make the recommendation more precise.

The text frames MinHash as a security primitive ("MinHash security relies on…"), but MinHash here is used for similarity/dedup quality and reproducibility. If the concern is adversarial robustness, it’s worth stating that explicitly and calling out the determinism tradeoff instead of implying cryptographic security properties.

Finding 4 describes a temp-file leak on exceptions, but `graphify/google_workspace.py` currently unlinks `tmp_path` in a `finally` block for each of these code paths. Updating the heading/severity to reflect that this is already mitigated will prevent readers from treating this as an open issue.

This section states there is "no cleanup guarantee" for the NamedTemporaryFile usage, but the current code wraps each tmp file in a try/finally and calls `tmp_path.unlink(missing_ok=True)`. The narrative and fix recommendation should be updated to match the current implementation.

Potential regression for portable manifests on macOS: manifest keys are NFC-normalized before being passed to `_to_relative_for_storage()`, but that helper computes `os.path.relpath(p, Path(root).resolve())`. If `Path(root).resolve()` is NFD (macOS default) and `k` is NFC, `relpath` will treat an in-root file as out-of-root and return a path starting with `..`, causing the key to be kept absolute. This undermines the `root=` portability guarantee (#777) specifically for non-ASCII roots.

Consider NFC-normalizing *both* `p` and the resolved root inside `_to_relative_for_storage()` (or otherwise ensuring both operands use the same normalization form) before calling `os.path.relpath`.

The new manifest-key normalization logic (`_nfc` + normalized lookups in `load_manifest`/`detect_incremental`) addresses #2221, but there doesn’t appear to be an automated test covering the NFC/NFD manifest mismatch scenario (unlike the existing Office sidecar NFC/NFD hash test). Adding a unit test that writes a manifest with NFD keys and verifies `detect_incremental()` reports 0 new / 0 deleted for the same logical files would prevent regressions.

good catch — pushed a follow-up. `_to_relative_for_storage` now NFC's both the key and `Path(root).resolve()` before `relpath`, and the absolute re-anchor join NFC's the result too. should keep the #777 relative keys intact on macOS non-ASCII roots.
fair point. kept this PR to the detect.py fix only for now — happy to add a regression test in a follow-up if maintainers want it in-tree.

This Stage 2 carve-out prevents `.env.example`-style names from being marked sensitive, but `classify_file()` only looks at `path.suffix` and does not recognize `.example`/`.sample`/`.template`/`.dist` as a supported extension. As a result, these files will likely move from `skipped_sensitive` to `unclassified` (still not added to `result["files"]`), so they still won’t be indexed into the graph. Consider adding a targeted `classify_file()` special-case for `.env*`/`.envrc*` template names (treat as `FileType.DOCUMENT`) rather than globally allowing all `*.example` files.

Runtime check of the version gate, for the record: with `mcp` 1.29.0 the `Server` class still exposes the decorator methods (1.x path taken); with `mcp` 2.0.0 they are gone and `Server.__init__` exposes the `on_list_tools`/`on_call_tool`/`on_list_resources`/`on_read_resource` callbacks (2.x path taken). Both branches of the `hasattr(Server, "list_tools")` guard are exercised.

In `architecture_definition`, the `implements` edge targets `_make_id(entity_name)` while `entity_declaration` nodes use `_make_id(stem, name)`. This creates a second, disconnected entity node and prevents the architecture→entity link from resolving even when the entity is declared in the same file.

`source <file>` edges currently target `_make_id(filename)` and also create a new node for that id. File nodes elsewhere use `_make_id(str(path))`, so these edges won’t connect to the sourced file’s file-node (and creating a node here risks id collisions once you switch to path-based ids). Consider resolving the sourced path and emitting the edge directly to the file-node id, using `target_file` when the file exists on disk.

Looked into this properly — measured rather than reasoned about — and I'd like to decline it, for two independent reasons.

**The suggested edit is anchored on a function this path never calls.** It patches `_php_name_text` (`engine.py:579-586`), but the `scoped_call_expression` branch reads its scope through `_read_text(scope_node, source)` at `engine.py:4386`; `_php_name_text` is called only at `600`, `606`, `2715`, `2720` and `2734`. Applied literally, the edit changes `_php_collect_type_refs` and `_php_emit_base` and leaves relative-scope calls untouched — while removing the `references` edges that `function make(): static` currently mints for `static`/`self`/`parent`, as an unreviewed side effect.

**Applied as intended, it reintroduces the defect in a different place.** I patched the actual branch so a relative scope emits the *method* name as an unqualified callee, and re-ran extraction on a PHPUnit-shaped corpus (base class out of corpus, one unrelated in-corpus `setUp`). Baseline: 0 edges. With the change: one INFERRED `calls` edge, `FooTest::prepare()` → `App\Models\ServiceCategory::setUp()`. The raw call has `is_member_call=False`, so it is not skipped at `extract.py:5572` and is not claimed by any typed resolver — it falls to the shared normalized-label loop at `extract.py:5564+`, whose index keys `.setUp()` and `setUp()` identically, making a single same-named method anywhere in the corpus an unconditional single-candidate bind. That is the same fabricated-edge shape as the bug this commit fixes, aimed at a different label. A corpus with two same-named candidates produced 0 edges in both trees, so the damage lands precisely where the bind is most confident.

**And it cannot be resolved correctly at that point.** The raw-call record carries caller, callee, receiver and receiver type — no enclosing or base class. The `inherits` edges that would answer "which class does `parent` denote" are never consulted by that loop, so an unqualified callee can only be name-matched. Refusing is also what the pipeline already does with every PHP member call it cannot type (`extract.py:5572`), so this keeps the existing policy rather than introducing a new class of drop.

On "silently": fair as a description of runtime behaviour, and the drop has no diagnostic counter. It is not undocumented, though — four tests in `tests/test_php_relative_scope_calls.py` pin it (including a positive control that absolute scoped calls still resolve), and the changelog entry states it outright. Binding a relative scope to its real target needs a base-class-aware resolution pass; I've opened that as its own issue on our fork rather than land an edge that is wrong in a different direction, and I'm happy to pick it up here if you'd want it.

`json.dumps(..., ensure_ascii=False)` output is embedded directly into a `<script>` block. If `elements` contains U+2028 or U+2029 (possible from user-provided idea text), the generated HTML can become invalid JavaScript and fail to load. Use ASCII escapes (default `ensure_ascii=True`) for safe script embedding.

`note_uri` is accepted as an arbitrary string and later rendered into an `<a href=...>` in the generated HTML. If a caller passes an untrusted value (e.g. `javascript:`), this becomes an injection vector. Since this workflow is intended to link back to Obsidian, validate that the URI uses the `obsidian://` scheme before building elements.

The `_safe_stem` validation message says the title must contain at least one letter or number, but the current check only ensures the string is non-empty after stripping characters. Titles like "---" will pass even though they contain no letters/numbers. Align the validation logic with the error message (use `str.isalnum()` so non-ASCII letters are accepted too).

The concept ranking only checks `weighedDegree` (and falls back to `degree`). Many APIs use `weightedDegree`; if InfraNodus returns that key, ranking and node sizing will silently degrade. Consider accepting both spellings to be resilient to response variations.

`_write_new` uses a predictable temp filename (`.{name}.tmp`). If an attacker (or a stale filesystem state) pre-creates that temp path as a symlink, `write_text` can write outside the intended directory before the atomic replace. Use `tempfile.mkstemp` (or similar) to create a unique temp file safely in the target directory.

`graphify.idea` imports `graphify.security._build_opener`, but the leading underscore marks it as private to the `security` module. Importing it from another module makes internal API changes harder and weakens encapsulation. Consider promoting this to a public helper (e.g. `build_opener` / `safe_open`) and using that here.

The CLI help output contains non-ASCII characters (e.g. the “crate→crate” arrow elsewhere in `--help`), and `_run_cli()` forces UTF-8 output. Decoding `r.stdout` using the parent process locale via `text=True` can fail under an ASCII locale (UnicodeDecodeError) or produce mojibake. Make the test locale-independent by decoding as UTF-8 (and optionally using errors='replace').

This assertion is very permissive: it would still pass if the `provider` command line were removed but some other help text happened to contain the substring "provider". Asserting the command prefix (e.g. "  provider ") makes the regression test more precise.

The subcommand list ordering here doesn’t match the CLI’s own usage string (`graphify provider [add|list|show|remove]` in `cli.py`). Keeping the same order reduces future drift and makes it easier for users to correlate `--help` with the error usage output.

The C# witness test only asserts that no duplicate keys appear, but it will still pass if extraction regresses and emits *zero* parameter-type reference edges. Add an assertion that a Widget parameter-type references edge exists exactly once so the test actually exercises the behavior it’s meant to protect.

Deduping edges by keeping the full `json.dumps(...)` string in `_seen_edge_payloads` can be unnecessarily memory-heavy on large extractions. Using compact separators (and matching the canonical JSON style already used elsewhere) reduces the size of every stored payload string without changing the dedupe semantics.

The dependency target node is being marked as `type="module"` but `file_type="concept"`. Elsewhere, module anchor nodes are emitted with `file_type="code"` (e.g. Swift module anchors in `extractors/engine.py`), and some downstream symbol/indexing utilities gate on `file_type == "code"`. Using `concept` here risks these module anchors being filtered out in code-centric views/indices, undermining the intended “imports bind to module anchor” behavior.
